objdescid.origination: Thomas Butts, Jr.etcher, engraver. Both Blake and the senior Thomas Butts may have had some role in executing this plate; see the introductory essay for more information.

provenance.name: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C.
provenance.note: Thomas Butts, Jr., who engraved the plate; probably by inheritance in 1862 to his son, Frederick J. Butts (1833-1905); possibly one of the prints sold anonymously, but probably from the Butts family, Sotheby's, 22 March 1910, lot 447, "a number of Engravings and Drawings, by William Blake and some by T. Butts" (£19.10s. to the dealer James Robson, possibly acting for William A. White); White by no later than 1919; with the dealer A. S. W. Rosenbach no later than 1927; given by Rosenbach to Lessing J. Rosenwald, with four other impressions from the plate, in July 1927; given by Rosenwald to the National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C., in 1943.

repository.institution: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C.

desc.objtitle: Lear and Cordelia, impression 4G, Object 1 (Essick XLV)

objnote.p: This impression is in the fourth state of four. The pencil inscriptions were very probably written by a member of the Butts family.

illustration.illusdesc: Two figures are grouped closely together in an oval composition. Only their upper bodies are depicted. On the left, Lear, the male figure, stands or sits with his body forward and turns his head to the right to look at Cordelia with fear or concern. His face is shown in profile. He bends his left arm to point to the left at something outside of the frame. A cloth may drape horizontally from his right shoulder over his shirt. He has long hair, a long beard, and furrowed eyebrows. He may be frowning. On the right, the female figure, Cordelia, stands or sits slightly behind Lear. She may be listening to him. She turns her body and her face slightly to the left to look at Lear. Her right arm bends upward and she rests her face against her clenched fist. Her mouth is closed and she wears a veil or cloak that drapes from the top of her head and over her long hair. Dense crosshatching darkens the background. The male might by Prospero and the female might be Miranda, both characters from Shakespeare's The Tempest, instead of Lear and Cordelia.

component.illusobjdesc: A male figure, Lear, stands or sits on the left. Only his upper body is depicted. He faces forward and turns his head to the right to look at Cordelia with fear or concern. His face is shown in profile. He bends his left arm to point to the left at something outside of the frame. He wears a dark shirt and a white or light-colored cloth drapes horizontally from his right shoulder. He has long hair, a long beard, and furrowed eyebrows. He may be frowning. He looks at the figure to his right. This might be Prospero, a character from Shakespeare's The Tempest, instead of Lear.

On the right, the female figure, Cordelia, stands or sits slightly behind Lear. Only her upper body is depicted. She turns her body and her face slightly to the left to look at Lear. She may be listening to him. Her eyes are raised slightly to look at him. Her right arm bends upward and she rests her head against her clenched fist. Her mouth is closed and she wears a veil or cloak that drapes over her head. Her long, wavy hair falls over her shoulders. This might be Miranda, a character from Shakespeare's The Tempest, instead of Cordelia.
Both figures are set before a dark, heavily shadowed background.
